openssl is a library that comes with a command line interface you can use to analyze the state and metadata on an SSL (secure socket layer) certificate.

but it's not really ssl anymore, it's tls (transport layer security) -- techies just historically called it ssl and it still sticks. potato pototto.

a csr is a certificate signing request that is the first step of getting an ssl certificate going. it includes things like the common name (domain.com), alt names (www.domain.com, somethingiwant.domain.com), the city/state/country/admin email, etc. -- in the case of legit ssl, this is passed to a certificate authority along with some money (or in some cases it's free as long as you set up dns records or an http page or code snippet to prove your ownership of the domain). when you make a csr you keep in your hands what is called a private key. this key is installed server-side and is never to be leaked - if it is, you have to revoke your cert, or someone can use it to decrypt your traffic

once the CA has the csr they can issue a certificate, which is the other 'half' of the puzzle - you have your private key and your cert. so you install those on your webserver. in some cases like with extended validation or EV certs, the CA also has additional certs that they provide to offer more validation in the chain - that way if the CA is compromised they can revoke their certs, and that breaks the chain, which causes your cert to stop working. extra validation.

so anyways these certs that you order for money or for free are usually good for a year or multiple years (that's gonna change this year -- major web browsers are gonna start ignoring certs that are valid for more than a year, in some sort of effort to show the community that periodic renewal is more trusted than long-standing certs as logic dictates that the longer you have that cert, the more likely it is that someone could compromise it).

so how do you check this shit on your end?

well, you can install and use the sslscan tool -- sslscan site.com -- pretty simple

you can use the openssl command: openssl s_client -connect site.com:443

you can click the little lock icon in your browser's address bar and hit view certificate and look at the issuer and the dates on it, as well as the common name.
